passage:
Dear Sabiha Khala,
Thank you for calling after Ammi told you about my first period. Before that week I felt so strange. Dadi said I mustn't touch the pickle jars and must never let Asif Bhai know, and I started hiding my pads in my school bag. I felt dirty, and also oddly important, like everyone was suddenly watching me grow up.
You told me it's a normal, healthy part of growing up, nothing unclean, and nothing to be ashamed of. You said faith has its own rules about prayer, and that is different from shame. Then you talked to Ammi. Now she keeps supplies openly in the bathroom cupboard, and yesterday even Asif Bhai just asked if I wanted a hot water bottle.
Love,
Rukhsar

qa.q: Where does Ammi keep supplies now?
qa.a: Openly in the bathroom cupboard.

qa.q: What did Rukhsar feel in the week before Khala's call?
qa.a: Rukhsar felt ashamed and 'dirty', hiding pads, yet also oddly important, as if suddenly grown up and watched.

qa.q: What did Khala's call change, and why did it help?
qa.a: Khala gave simple facts, said periods are nothing unclean or shameful, separated faith rules from shame, and spoke to Ammi, so secrecy gave way to openness.

qa.q: How does Asif Bhai seem to see it now?
qa.a: Asif Bhai seems to treat it as ordinary, kindly offering a hot water bottle instead of it being a secret.

grounding: Shows a girl told to follow restrictions and keep secrecy after her first period, who feels both shamed and important until health facts and respect replace the stigma.

passage:
Mehak's first period had started on Sunday, and by Wednesday she knew all the new rules: don't enter the puja room, don't touch the pickle jar, sit apart at dinner. Her Nani said it was so she could rest. It felt like being dirty.

At school she hadn't told anyone, not even Arohi. In the biology lab, when the teacher said, "Today, menstruation," two boys sniggered, and Mehak went red to her ears.

Mrs Pinto stopped the class. "This is a normal body process that half of you will have and all of you should understand. Nothing about it is dirty or funny." Then she explained it plainly, with diagrams, and said anyone could come to her with questions.

At lunch Mehak told Arohi. Arohi squeezed her hand. "Mine started in June. Same kind of rules at my house. Let's go and ask Mrs Pinto together."

qa.q: What rules had Mehak learned by Wednesday?
qa.a: Don't enter the puja room, don't touch the pickle jar, sit apart at dinner.

qa.q: How did Mehak feel about the new rules at home?
qa.a: Mehak felt ashamed and set apart; though Nani said it was for rest, it felt like being dirty.

qa.q: How did Mrs Pinto replace stigma with facts?
qa.a: She stopped the sniggering, said plainly it is a normal body process, explained it with diagrams, and invited questions.

qa.q: What was it like for Arohi when Mehak told her?
qa.a: Arohi felt close and supportive, sharing that hers started in June and offering to go to Mrs Pinto together.

grounding: Shows a girl told to follow restrictions after her first period, feeling shamed, and a teacher and friend replacing stigma with plain facts and respect.

passage:
Dear Maria,

You asked why I missed school last week and why there are photos of me in a silk saree on my aunt's status. Okay. It was a puberty ceremony. My first period started, and in our family that means a big function.

Part of it felt amazing: a new saree, jasmine in my hair, all the aunties blessing me, gifts. I felt important, like a grown-up.

Part of it felt awful. The whole family knowing about my body. Sitting in a separate room for days. My cousin asking loudly if I was "impure now".

On the last night Amma sat with me. She said the function was to celebrate me, not shame me, and that she'd keep the separate-room custom short. She gave me a book about what's happening in my body and said I can ask her anything.

I still feel mixed, but less weird. Please don't show anyone this letter.

Chandrika

qa.q: What did Chandrika wear at the ceremony?
qa.a: Chandrika wore a new silk saree, with jasmine in the hair.

qa.q: What mixed feelings did Chandrika have about the ceremony?
qa.a: Chandrika felt important and grown-up with the blessings and gifts, but embarrassed that everyone knew and hurt by being kept apart.

qa.q: How did Amma help replace secrecy with respect?
qa.a: She said the function celebrated Chandrika rather than shamed her, kept the old custom short, and gave a book of facts with an open invitation to ask anything.

qa.q: How might Maria react to this letter?
qa.a: Maria may be curious and surprised, and likely feel trusted that Chandrika shared something so private.

grounding: Shows a girl whose first period is marked by a ceremony and restrictions, feeling shamed, protected and important at once, and a parent turning to facts and respect.

passage:
You want to know what it was like? Okay. I'm Rehana, and I was twelve and at my cousin's wedding in Hyderabad when it started.

My Khala pulled me into a side room and whispered everything like it was a crime: "Don't tell anyone. Don't let your brothers see. Wrap the packet in newspaper." I felt like I'd done something wrong. For a year I hid pads in my maths box.

My friend Pallavi was the one who said, "Why are you hiding them? It's just a period." Her mother is a nurse. She sat us both down at their dining table and explained it all with a diagram on a napkin: what's happening, why it's healthy, what's normal, and when to check with a doctor.

I went home and told Ammi I didn't want to hide it any more. She was quiet, then said, "My mother made me hide it too. You don't have to."

Now they sit in the bathroom cupboard, like a normal thing.

qa.q: Where did Rehana hide pads for a year?
qa.a: Rehana hid pads in the maths box.

qa.q: How did Rehana feel after Khala's whispered instructions?
qa.a: Rehana felt ashamed, as if something wrong had been done, and kept it hidden for a year.

qa.q: What helped replace secrecy with facts?
qa.a: Pallavi's mother explaining plainly with a diagram what is happening and what is normal, and then Rehana telling Ammi openly.

qa.q: What might Ammi have felt when Rehana said no more hiding?
qa.a: Ammi seemed quietly moved, remembering being made to hide it herself, and relieved to let Rehana stop.

grounding: Shows a girl taught to hide her first period as shameful, and adults replacing that secrecy with health facts and respect.

passage:
Day one: Leela, thirteen, got her first period at home in Madurai. Paati said she mustn't enter the kitchen or touch the pickle jars, and must sit on a separate mat. Leela felt dirty and confused, and also strangely important, because all the aunties phoned.
Day three: At school, Dr Wasim, the school doctor, gave the girls' health talk. He showed a diagram and said periods are a normal, healthy part of growing up, and nothing to hide. A girl asked if touching pickles really spoils them. The class giggled. Dr Wasim smiled. "No. That's a belief, not a fact." Leela felt her shoulders loosen.
Day six: At home, Leela sat with Amma and told her what the doctor said. "I don't want to feel dirty." Amma was quiet, then said, "Neither did I." That evening Amma told Paati the mat could go, and they kept only the small puja, with sweets.

qa.q: What did Paati say Leela mustn't touch?
qa.a: The pickle jars.

qa.q: How did Leela feel on day one?
qa.a: She felt dirty and confused, and also strangely important because all the aunties phoned.

qa.q: What helped replace secrecy with respect in Leela's home?
qa.a: The doctor's health facts at school, and Leela talking openly with Amma, who then spoke to Paati.

qa.q: How might Amma have felt when Leela said she didn't want to feel dirty?
qa.a: Amma probably felt moved and understanding, remembering feeling the same way when she was young.

grounding: It illustrates a girl told to observe restrictions after her first period who feels both shamed and important, and how health facts and respect replace stigma.
